unit.name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
question_text: What is the effect of (i) intensity of light (ii) potential on photoelectric current?

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students, physics section, Ch.12 (printed p.43; the book's heading misprints 'photelectric'). The book prints no exam-year citations for this chapter. The 2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked physically: at fixed frequency the photocurrent is directly proportional to intensity (straight line through the origin); with anode potential the current rises to a saturation value, and under a retarding potential it falls to zero at the stopping potential −V₀; for a given frequency V₀ is independent of intensity (the three curves I₃ > I₂ > I₁ share one −V₀) — all consistent with the standard NCERT treatment. This question covers the laws of photoelectric emission at LAQ grade in most other syllabuses; it is kept as the 4-mark SAQ this book prints.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter · 4 marks

steps.label: Effect of intensity
lines: (i) Keep the frequency of the incident
radiation fixed and increase the intensity
of the light. The number of photons striking
the surface per unit area per second
increases, so the number of photoelectrons
emitted per second increases in the same way.
The photoelectric current is directly
proportional to the intensity of the
incident radiation:
The graph of current against intensity is a
straight line through the origin O.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The mechanism (more photons, more photoelectrons) plus the proportionality and its straight-line graph.
steps.why: One photon frees at most one electron, so doubling the photon arrival rate doubles the electron emission rate — that one-to-one link is the whole reason the graph is a straight line through the origin.
common_mistakes: Saying higher intensity gives faster electrons. Intensity changes how MANY electrons are emitted, not their maximum speed.
Drawing the line starting above the origin. Zero intensity means zero current, so the line passes through O.

recall.must_convey: That at a fixed frequency the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the radiation.

steps.memory_tip: Intensity counts photons, and photons count electrons: i ∝ I.

steps.label: Current against intensity
steps.margin_note: A small sketch is enough: both axes labelled, and the line starting at O.
steps.why: The straight line through the origin is the picture of i ∝ I — a line that misses O would claim current with no light.
common_mistakes: Curving the line. Direct proportionality draws a straight line.
Leaving the axes unlabelled. An unlabelled sketch shows nothing.

recall.must_convey: That the graph is a straight line through the origin with current on one axis and intensity on the other.

steps.memory_tip: One line, from O, going up — that is the whole intensity graph.

steps.label: Effect of potential
lines: (ii) Now keep the intensity fixed and make
the anode A more and more positive. The
photoelectric current increases at first,
then reaches a maximum value and stays there.
This maximum is the saturation current: every
photoelectron emitted by the cathode C now
reaches the anode A.
Next make the anode negative instead. The
negative anode repels the photoelectrons, so
the current decreases. At one value of the
retarding potential the current becomes zero.
This value is the stopping potential V₀.
For a fixed frequency, a higher intensity
gives a higher saturation current, but the
stopping potential stays the same: V₀ is
independent of the intensity and depends
only on the frequency of the radiation.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Saturation current for the positive side, stopping potential for the negative side — and the sentence that V₀ does not change with intensity.
steps.why: The positive side counts electrons (all of them arrive at saturation); the negative side measures their maximum kinetic energy (eV₀). Intensity changes the count but not the energy, so the curves share one −V₀.
common_mistakes: Saying the current keeps rising with anode potential. It stops rising at the saturation current.
Making V₀ depend on intensity. The three curves for I₃ > I₂ > I₁ all reach zero at the same −V₀.
Writing that below V₀ the current is maximum. At the stopping potential the current is zero.

recall.must_convey: That the current saturates at positive potentials, falls to zero at the stopping potential, and V₀ is independent of intensity.
accept: current becomes zero at the stopping potential
stopping potential does not depend on intensity

steps.memory_tip: Positive side: count saturates. Negative side: zero at −V₀. Intensity moves the first, never the second.

steps.label: Current against anode potential
steps.margin_note: Three curves for three intensities: separate saturation levels labelled I₁, I₂, I₃ at their right ends, and ONE common −V₀ where all three meet the axis.
steps.why: The figure carries both facts at once: higher intensity lifts the saturation level, while all three curves reach zero at the same stopping potential −V₀.
common_mistakes: Giving each curve its own stopping potential. For one frequency all the curves meet the axis at the same −V₀.
Letting the saturation levels touch. Draw them clearly separated and label each at its right end.

recall.must_convey: That the graph shows three curves saturating at I₃ > I₂ > I₁ and meeting the potential axis together at −V₀.
accept: three curves with one stopping potential
saturation levels I three greater than I two greater than I one

steps.memory_tip: Three plateaus on the right, one meeting point on the left.

insider_note: The sentence that separates answers is the last one: the stopping potential does not change with intensity — only the saturation current does.
